edges.effect_quant: A systematic review of 9 randomized trials including 1039 Crohn disease patients and 138 ulcerative colitis patients found an apparent Crohn disease benefit (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61-0.98) but no ulcerative colitis benefit (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.51-2.03); however, the two large EPIC Crohn trials totaling 738 patients showed no relapse reduction, and a 64-patient UC trial found only a transient early delay in relapse with identical 2-year cumulative relapse rates.
edges.population: patients with quiescent Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis enrolled in maintenance-of-remission omega-3 or fish-oil trials
edges.mechanism: Omega-3 fatty acids can shift eicosanoid balance away from arachidonic-acid-derived inflammatory mediators and may modulate mucosal cytokine signaling, but these biochemical effects have not translated reliably into durable clinical remission.
edges.summary: Omega-3 supplementation has looked promising mechanistically and in some smaller older IBD trials, but the overall remission-maintenance literature is mixed. The most credible interpretation is that any clinical benefit is small, inconsistent, and not robust enough to count on as a standalone maintenance strategy.
edges.caveats: Results differ by disease subtype, trial era, formulation, background medication use, and relapse definition. Publication bias and smaller positive studies likely inflated early enthusiasm, whereas the largest Crohn disease trials were convincingly negative.

evidence.citation: Turner D et al 2011 Inflamm Bowel Dis
